# What Is an AI Center of Excellence?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-center-of-excellence/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An AI center of excellence (CoE) is an internal team that sets the standards for how a company uses AI, decides which requests get built or bought first, runs pilots, and helps other teams build skills. Its purpose is to stop AI adoption from becoming either fragmented or ungoverned. Large firms staff it with data scientists, engineers and governance specialists; a 20 to 500 person firm can run one with two or three people, provided someone owns it and it has a written mandate.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## Key points

- Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework describes an AI CoE as an internal team of experts that "prevents fragmented or ungoverned AI adoption".
- The same guidance recommends starting centralised and evolving "from a centralized control to an advisory team" as adoption matures.
- In McKinsey's survey of 1,491 participants, published March 2025, risk, compliance and data governance were most often run through a fully centralised model such as a center of excellence.
- The same survey found 28% of respondents said their CEO oversees AI governance, and 17% their board.
- In the US public sector, OMB memo M-25-21 required agencies to name a Chief AI Officer within 60 days and, for larger agencies, convene an AI governance board within 90 days.

## What an AI center of excellence means

The term borrows from older centers of excellence for cloud or analytics: a small group concentrates expertise, writes the rules and helps everyone else adopt. Unlike a governance committee, it also does work, running pilots and publishing reusable assets. Unlike a central build team, done well, it does not build everything itself.

| An AI CoE is | It is not |
| --- | --- |
| The owner of AI standards, intake and the AI inventory | The only team allowed to use AI |
| A source of approved patterns and reusable assets | A queue every request must wait in |
| Accountable to an executive sponsor | A side project of the IT helpdesk |

## What it does

Microsoft's guidance lists eight responsibilities. They map well onto what a mid-size firm needs, with the scale adjusted.

| Responsibility | In a large enterprise | In a 20 to 500 person firm (illustrative) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AI strategy | Align AI with business goals; responsible AI policy | One page: where AI is used first and why |
| Skills | Learning pathways and hands-on labs | Role-based briefings and a literacy record |
| Pilots | Prioritised proofs of concept | One pilot at a time on the commercial line |
| Standards | Governance, security, bias and transparency reviews | [Acceptable use policy](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-acceptable-use-policy/), data rule, approval rules |
| Intake and prioritisation | Structured intake and an AI backlog | A shared list of requests with a monthly decision |
| Reusable assets | Checklists, templates, code libraries | Approved prompts, vendor question set, impact assessment template |
| Measure and report | Adoption, compliance and cycle-time KPIs | Quarterly note to leadership on uses, outcomes and incidents |
| Manage AI services (optional) | Model monitoring and lifecycle management | Usually left to vendors |

The skills row now carries a legal dimension for firms with EU exposure. Article 4 of the EU AI Act requires measures to support staff AI literacy; see [What is AI literacy?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-literacy/). A CoE is the natural owner of that record.

## How it is organised and how it evolves

Microsoft recommends a named CoE leader, executive sponsorship through a steering group with monthly reviews, and building on existing teams rather than creating a standalone one. Without sponsorship, it says, "the AI CoE can't enforce standards or drive organizational change."

Its guidance on evolution is the most useful part. Centralisation "at the onset accelerates AI adoption", but the CoE should move to an advisory role once governance can be built into platforms and daily operations. The warning signs it lists are approval delays, knowledge bottlenecks, and product teams and the CoE debating priorities instead of delivering value. The aim is to "replace the CoE gatekeeper model that blocks work with an advisory group that sets guardrails."

McKinsey's data points the same way. Risk, compliance and data governance are usually centralised; talent and adoption are more often hybrid, with some resources central and others in functions. Firms with under $500 million in revenue were more likely to centralise talent and adoption fully, which fits a small firm's reality: there are not enough specialists to distribute.

| Stage | Typical model | Sign it is time to move on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting | Centralised: the CoE approves and often delivers | Requests queue for weeks |
| Scaling | Hybrid: standards central, delivery in teams | Teams have their own capable owners |
| Mature | Advisory: CoE sets guardrails and reviews exceptions | Governance runs inside normal approval routes |

## Common mistakes

- **No executive owner.** A CoE without a sponsor publishes standards nobody follows.
- **Building instead of enabling.** If the CoE delivers every use, it becomes the bottleneck it was meant to prevent.
- **Measuring activity.** Counting pilots says little; recording which uses changed an outcome says more.
- **Starting everywhere.** **lowob**'s view is to start on the commercial line, where outcomes are measurable.

## The **lowob** view

In **lowob**'s terms, a CoE's lasting job is to own the record, not the tools: the AI inventory, the autonomy level and approver for each use, the decision log and the outcomes written back each quarter. The wiring can be rented and builds can move to teams. The record is what lets the CoE step back to an advisory role without losing control. Gateway 0 in The Build Order, which names an owner before any tool is bought, is the smallest version of a CoE.

## lowob takeaways

- **Mandate and owner first.** A named leader and an executive sponsor matter more than headcount.
- **Start central, plan to step back.** Guidance recommends moving from control to an advisory role.
- **Own the record.** Inventory, approvals and outcomes are the CoE's durable output.
- **Small is fine.** Two or three people with a written mandate can run one in a mid-size firm.

## Common questions

### What is an AI center of excellence?

An internal team that sets AI standards, prioritises requests, runs pilots and builds skills, so that AI adoption is neither fragmented nor ungoverned.

### Who should be in an AI center of excellence?

An executive sponsor, a named leader, business leads who know the use cases, and technical, security and governance expertise, drawn from existing teams where possible.

### Does a small company need an AI CoE?

It needs the functions, not a department: an owner, an inventory, standards, intake and a record of decisions. Two or three people part-time can cover them.

### What is the difference between an AI CoE and an AI governance committee?

A governance committee approves and oversees. A CoE also does work: pilots, reusable assets, skills and support for teams.
